title: Finding the Milky Way on a starry mountain night
description: On a clear, dark night far from town lights, a pale band crosses the sky. That band is our own galaxy seen edge-on — and mountains are one of the best places to find it.

body.heading: A band of a hundred billion suns
paragraphs: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy, and we live inside one of its arms. Looking along the flat disc of the galaxy, we see stars so numerous and distant that their light merges into a glowing band. Dark lanes in the band are not empty sky — they are clouds of dust blocking the light behind them.
The band is brightest toward the constellation Sagittarius, where we look toward the galaxy's crowded centre.

body.heading: How to give yourself the best chance
paragraphs: Choose a moonless night, get as far from streetlights as you can, and let your eyes adjust for at least twenty minutes without looking at a phone. High, dry places — mountain viewpoints above the haze — show the band at its sharpest.
What looks like a faint cloud is neither cloud nor mist: it does not move or change shape through the night, because it is the structure of the galaxy itself, turning with the sky.

takeaway: The pale band over dark mountains is our galaxy seen from inside: a hundred billion stars merged into one river of light.
